newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: HK stock exchange to stay independent -official.
newsitem.headline: HK stock exchange to stay independent -official.

text.p: Hong Kong's stock exchange will remain independent after the British colony returns to Chinese rule next year, a senior exchange official said on Friday.
He also did not expect any regulatory changes at the bourse after the June 1997 handover.
"I believe the Hong Kong and China exchanges will continue to act independently," Herbert Hui, deputy chief executive of the Stock Exchange of Hong Kong, told Reuters.
"We all have our own separate features," he said.

"Hong Kong, Shenzhen and Shanghai are communicating with one another once every three months to discuss developments," Hui said." But at the same time, all three of us have separate roles to play towards the 21st century."
Hui was attending a two-day Asia-Pacific Equity Markets Outlook 1997 conference.
Hui dismissed concerns that there may be fundamental changes in the Hong Kong stock exchange after the island reverts to Chinese sovereignty after more than 150 years of colonial rule.

"I don't see any fundamental changes (in either rules or regulations) in the Hong Kong stock exchange because a lot of the thoughts and ideas to cater for 1997 were first contemplated back in 1992," Hui said.
"Over the years, we have been implementing these changes in order to ensure that we can face the challenges of the handover," Hui said.

Among these changes was a listing rule in 1993 that took into account the legal and accounting differences between mainland China and Hong Kong, paving the way for Chinese enterprises to list in Hong Kong.

To-date, Hong Kong has helped Chinese companies raise US$3.5 billion in capital. These figures do not include the number of Hong Kong-incorporated companies controlled by China, or so-called "red-chips." He was optimistic that Hong Kong would continue to help Chinese enterprises raise capital.

Hui also dismissed concerns that recent resignation of the exchange's chief executive officer, Paul Chow Man-yiu, on speculation that his relationship with the exchange chairman Edgar Cheng Wai-yin had broken down, has negatively affected the exchange's image.
"Obviously, like any other stock exchanges, we have our share of staff turnover. That is not a scandal. I think the image of the exchange is still very positive," Hui said.
Chow will leave on January 31 after giving six-months notice.
